output.query: psychogenic non-epileptic seizures diagnosis and management

results.key_finding: A documented diagnosis of psychogenic non-epileptic seizures requires video-EEG capture of a typical event without epileptiform activity before, during or after it, together with a history and semiology consistent with PNES; lower levels of certainty rest on history, witnessed semiology and routine EEG.
results.title: Minimum requirements for the diagnosis of psychogenic nonepileptic seizures: a staged approach

output.summary: Video-EEG capture of a typical event without an electrographic correlate gives the documented level of diagnostic certainty for PNES [LaFrance_2013]. Prolonged PNES mistaken for status epilepticus leads to repeated benzodiazepines, intubation and anaesthetic infusions, with iatrogenic harm. Psychological treatment, mostly CBT-informed, is the approach with trial evidence. Epilepsy and PNES coexist in a minority of patients, so each event type needs its own characterization.

action_criteria.rationale: Glucose, electrolyte, renal and hepatic derangements are reversible causes of seizures and decide the ASM and its dose; lamotrigine level because she takes it; toxicology because the cause is not yet evident; beta-hCG in a woman of reproductive age; prolactin and lactate soon after the event help separate a generalized convulsion from a non-epileptic event, though normal values do not exclude an epileptic seizure (CK rises only hours later) [Brophy_2012; LaFrance_2013].

prohibited_recommendations: Do not escalate to anaesthetic infusion or intubation for PNES [LaFrance_2013].
Do not load a second-line ASM or repeat benzodiazepines for events that video-EEG shows have no electrographic correlate.
Do not dismiss the patient: PNES is a real disorder that needs treatment and follow-up.
Do not prescribe valproate: she is planning a pregnancy.
required_recommendations: Base the diagnosis on video-EEG capture of the typical events (no electrographic correlate, preserved posterior rhythm) before any escalation of antiseizure treatment [LaFrance_2013].

If epileptic status cannot be excluded at the bedside before the video-EEG, a single adequately dosed benzodiazepine is acceptable (IV lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg, maximum 4 mg), without repeating it or adding a second-line ASM while semiology and video-EEG indicate PNES [Glauser_2016; LaFrance_2013].
Communicate the diagnosis of a functional (dissociative) event clearly and without blame, and arrange psychological treatment with her therapist or neuropsychiatry.
Continue lamotrigine 200 mg twice daily for JME without dose change (level 8.4 mcg/mL).
Address the precipitants (her mother's illness, night shifts) and screen for a PTSD or mood exacerbation and suicidality.

avoided_actions.rationale: No clinical suspicion of cardiac source of embolus or cardiogenic seizure; routine echo is not indicated in SE workup absent cardiac findings.
No suspicion of arrhythmogenic syncope or cardiac comorbidity precipitating SE; routine telemetry beyond standard ICU monitoring adds cost without yield.
Amyloid PET has no role in acute SE evaluation; dementia biomarker imaging does not change acute management.
Carotid duplex is for ischemic stroke workup; SE without focal vascular suspicion does not warrant carotid imaging.
Polysomnography studies sleep disorders and has no role in the acute evaluation of status epilepticus.
No infectious or autoimmune signs; LP not indicated.

patient.history_present_illness: A 38-year-old Hispanic female nurse was brought to the emergency department by her colleague after prolonged unresponsive episodes at their hospital unit. The patient had been at work when she suddenly became unresponsive and collapsed. Her colleague reported that she appeared to have rhythmic shaking of both arms for several minutes, then appeared to 'wake up' briefly, then became unresponsive again with more subtle rhythmic movements of the legs. Total duration of apparent seizure-like activity was over 30 minutes before EMS arrived. She has a known diagnosis of epilepsy diagnosed 8 years ago with generalized tonic-clonic seizures, now well-controlled on lamotrigine for the past 3 years without a breakthrough seizure. The colleague noted she had been under extreme stress recently — her mother was hospitalized with cancer last week, and she had been working 12-hour night shifts. The colleague is also aware the patient has a history of psychogenic non-epileptic seizures (PNES), diagnosed 2 years ago after video-EEG monitoring, and has been in therapy. On EMS arrival, she was unresponsive with eyes closed, making occasional moaning sounds. On ED arrival, 35 minutes after onset, she continues with intermittent bilateral arm trembling with eyes closed. She is not responding to commands. Blood was drawn on ED arrival, including a lamotrigine level.

neurological_exam.additional: Semiological features: eyes closed throughout, active eye closure when opened, waxing-waning intensity of movements, pelvic thrusting noted intermittently, head turning side to side. No post-ictal confusion period after movements resolve.

neurological_exam.mental_status: Appears unresponsive with eyes closed. Intermittent moaning. When the examiner attempts to open the eyelids, she actively closes them. Occasional purposeful-appearing arm movements.
neurological_exam.motor: Bilateral rhythmic arm trembling that waxes and wanes. Movements irregular in amplitude and frequency. No sustained tonic posturing. No Jacksonian march.
neurological_exam.reflexes: 2+ throughout. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally. No Babinski.
neurological_exam.sensory: Appears not to respond to noxious stimuli; limb withdrawal is inconsistent between trials.
